newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: ASEAN nod seen as boost for Cambodian stability.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN nod seen as boost for Cambodian stability.

text.p: Cambodia on Saturday warmly welcomed the Association of Southeast Nations (ASEAN) decision to admit it to the grouping in July, and some analysts said they were hopeful the move would be a catalyst for political stability.
Foreign ministers in the seven-member group decided in Kuala Lumpur to admit Cambodia, Burma and Laos at their meeting in July, not at an ASEAN summit meeting in December.
"Oh good, that's good for Cambodia," Information Minister Ieng Mouly told Reuters after hearing the news.
"Now we'll be part of the region, we can play a role in the region. We can contribute and particapate," he said.
"It's the best news of the year," said Kao Kim Hourn, director of the the Cambodian Institute for Co-operation and Peace think tank.

A bitter feud between the two leaders of Cambodia's coalition government over power-sharing and other issues has led to considerable tension and a deadlock in parliament, preventing the passing of key legislation needed for ASEAN membership.
ASEAN currently comprises Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, and Vietnam.
There were suggestions in Phnom Penh that the admission of Cambodia and the other two countries might be delayed until December, partly because of the political instability.
"I think this means they didn't take into consideration the internal problems," Ieng Mouly said.

Neither First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh nor his co-premier and political rival, Hun Sen, were immediately available for comment. But aides of both men welcomed the news that Cambodia would become a full member of ASEAN in July.
"He's very happy, it's a good day for Cambodia," said Kong Vibol, a press officer in Ranariddh's party.
"This is a good thing for Cambodia. It's fair and it can help stability in the region," Prak Sokhonn, an aide to Hun Sen told Reuters.
Analysts said the immediate benefits of joining ASEAN would be political rather than economic, with the possibility that membership of the group could help ease domestic political tension.
"It will be a catalyst for peace and stability in Cambodia," said Kao Kim Hourn.
"Our leaders will have to be more compromising, more flexible. Now we cannot operate in the sphere of Cambodia alone. Now we're in the sphere of ASEAN," he said.
Cambodia's membership of ASEAN could enable other members of the group to put greater pressure on Cambodia's leaders to resolve their disputes, a diplomat said.
"It will be that the other ASEAN members can now put pressure on the Cambodians, not necessarily that the Cambodian leaders will be more moderate," the diplomat said.

Membership of the dynamic regional group could also help Cambodia shed once and for all its "killing fields" image of death and destruction earned during the bloody 1970s Khmer Rouge rule and a subsequent decade-long war, diplomats and analysts said.

"Cambodia now cannot just be identified with the killing fields, all the negative images," said Kao Kim Hourn. "Now it can be identified with this fast-growing, dynamic region. Cambodia is now a part of that."

Officials said Cambodia would reap long-term economic gains from membership in ASEAN and its free trade area, though in the short-term there would have to be some difficult restructuring, particularly in the tax system and export sector, before the financial rewards began to flow.
